cards.t: All humans die.
Socrates is human.
Socrates is very famous.
cards.why: Fame has nothing to do with dying. This premise doesn't get you to the conclusion.

cards.t: All philosophers think a lot.
cards.why: Thinking isn't the point here. You need something that links Socrates to dying.

cards.t: Lots of people died before Socrates.
cards.why: Lots of people dying isn't logical proof that everyone will. That's generalizing from examples.

levels.win: This is the most famous syllogism in history: a general rule (all humans) + a specific case (Socrates is one of them) = a conclusion that must be true if both premises are true.

cards.t: If it rains, the ground gets wet.
It rained.
If the ground is wet, then it rained.
cards.why: That's the rule flipped, and it isn't always true: a garden hose can wet the ground too. It also doesn't prove the conclusion.

cards.t: The sky is cloudy.
cards.why: Clouds don't mean it actually rained.

cards.t: People opened their umbrellas.
cards.why: That's a sign, not proof. People might open them just in case.

levels.win: "If A, then B" + "A happened" = "B happened." It's the simplest rule in logic, and one of the strongest.

cards.t: If it rains, the ground gets wet.
The ground is bone dry.
The weather forecast said no rain.
cards.why: That's a trustworthy source, but it isn't logical proof. Forecasts can be wrong.

cards.t: It's hot today.
cards.why: Heat doesn't logically rule out rain.

cards.t: The ground is wet.
cards.why: That's the opposite of what you need, and it doesn't tell you anything about rain anyway.

levels.win: "If A, then B" + "B didn't happen" = "A didn't happen." If it had rained, the ground would be wet. The ground is dry, so it didn't rain.

levels.c: Maya will take the subway to work.

cards.t: Maya will get to work either by subway or by car.
Maya isn't driving today.
The subway is faster than driving.
cards.why: The subway being faster doesn't mean Maya will pick it.

cards.t: All of Maya's friends take the subway.
cards.why: What her friends do isn't evidence of what she'll choose.

cards.t: Maya loves the subway.
cards.why: Loving it isn't a guarantee. She could love it and still drive.

levels.win: "Either A or B" + "not B" = "A." But careful: this only works if those really are the only two options. If she could grab an Uber, the argument falls apart.

levels.c: If Jake studies, he'll get into his dream college.

cards.t: If Jake studies, he'll get great grades.
If Jake gets great grades, he'll get into his dream college.
Everyone who got into that college studied.
cards.why: This says the people who got in studied, not that anyone who studies gets in. The direction is backwards.

cards.t: Jake is really smart.
cards.why: Being smart isn't part of the chain you need.

cards.t: Jake has wanted to go there since he was a kid.
cards.why: Wanting something isn't enough to get you in.

levels.win: This is a chain: "A leads to B" and "B leads to C," so "A leads to C." Every link has to hold. If one link breaks, the whole chain breaks.

cards.t: Everyone on the swim team can swim.
Emma is in Room 12, and she's on the swim team.
Most people know how to swim.
cards.why: "Most" isn't "all." It doesn't guarantee anyone in this particular room can.

cards.t: The school has a swimming pool.
cards.why: Having a pool doesn't mean anyone can swim.

cards.t: Emma loves the beach.
cards.why: Loving the beach isn't the same as knowing how to swim.

levels.win: To prove that "someone" does something, one confirmed example is enough. Emma is in the room, and everyone on the team can swim, so someone in the room can swim.

levels.c: No animal in the room can fly.

cards.t: No cat can fly.
Every animal in the room is a cat.
I've never seen a cat fly.
cards.why: Not having seen something isn't proof it doesn't exist. That's an appeal to ignorance.

cards.t: Cats love to sleep a lot.
cards.why: Sleeping has nothing to do with flying.

cards.t: Cats usually don't have wings.
cards.why: "Usually" isn't enough to prove that not a single one does.

levels.win: A general negative rule ("no cat can fly") + everything in the room is a cat = no animal in the room can fly.

levels.c: Sarah will be late for work.

cards.t: If the train breaks down, Sarah will be late.
The train broke down this morning.
Sarah is always late.
cards.why: A habit isn't proof. She might show up early today.

cards.t: If Sarah is late, then the train broke down.
cards.why: That's the rule flipped, and it isn't true: she could be late for other reasons.

cards.t: Traffic is bad today.
cards.why: Traffic could make her late, but there's no rule here linking it to her.

levels.win: Same rule as before: "If A, then B, and A happened." But watch out for the flipped card. It's the most famous trap.

levels.c: Not everyone who wears glasses reads a lot.

cards.t: My uncle wears glasses.
My uncle has never read a book.
Most people who read a lot wear glasses.
cards.why: This is about readers, not about everyone who wears glasses.

cards.t: Glasses help you read.
cards.why: That doesn't prove or disprove that everyone who wears them reads.

cards.t: A lot of people say glasses make you look smart.
cards.why: Popular opinion isn't logical evidence.

levels.win: To knock down an "all…" statement, one counterexample is enough. Your uncle wears glasses and doesn't read = not everyone who wears glasses is a reader.

levels.c: We need to take the umbrella today.

cards.t: If it's raining, we'll get soaked without an umbrella.
If we'll get soaked without an umbrella, we need to take the umbrella.
It's raining right now.
The forecast said it might rain.
cards.why: "Might" isn't enough to prove "need to."

cards.t: It rained yesterday.
cards.why: Yesterday's rain says nothing about today.

cards.t: Everyone else has an umbrella.
cards.why: What the majority does isn't logical evidence.

levels.win: Boss level: a 3-link chain. Rain → soaked → umbrella. Every link has to be there. If even one is missing, the whole argument falls apart.
